items.summary: TinyML performs machine-learning inference under a milliwatt of power, breaking the power barrier that previously limited how widely machine intelligence could be distributed.
items.notes: "achieves ML inference under a milliWatt, and thereby breaks the traditional power barrier preventing widely distributed machine intelligence."

items.summary: On-device, near-sensor inference is valuable partly because it avoids the energy cost of wireless communication, which the authors state is far higher than compute cost at this scale (citing ref [5]).
items.notes: "By performing inference on-device, and near-sensor, TinyML enables greater responsiveness and privacy while avoiding the energy cost associated with wireless communication, which at this scale is far higher than that of compute [5]."

items.summary: MLPerf Tiny is described as the collaborative effort of more than 50 organizations from industry and academia.
items.notes: "the collaborative effort of more than 50 organizations from industry and academia and reflects the needs of the community."

items.summary: The suite measures accuracy, latency, and energy across four benchmarks: keyword spotting, visual wake words, image classification, and anomaly detection.

Low-power challenge: TinyML devices vary drastically in power draw, the scope of what counts as part of the power measurement is hard to define (data paths, pre-processing), and chip peripherals/firmware can affect measurements.

Limited-memory challenge: TinyML systems have roughly two orders of magnitude less memory than smartphone-class (GB) budgets; the benchmark itself risks not fitting; multiple quantization/precision levels must be represented.

value.memory_gap: ~2 orders of magnitude smaller than GB-class systems

items.summary: Hardware-heterogeneity challenge: devices range from general-purpose MCUs to novel architectures (event-based neural processors, memory-compute); a system under test may lack standard features like a clock or debug interface, so existing state-of-the-art benchmarks need reengineering.

Software-heterogeneity challenge: TinyML systems are tightly coupled to custom inference stacks and toolchains, especially with accelerators/DSPs, so a benchmark must balance optimality with portability and comparability with representativeness.
Cross-product challenge: there is diversity at every layer of the TinyML stack (Figure 1); a benchmark should let a user demonstrate benefit at any single layer.
CoreMark, the standard MCU-class benchmark, does not profile full programs and does not accurately represent machine-learning inference workloads.
items.notes: "CoreMark does not profile full programs, nor does it accurately represent machine learning inference workloads."

items.summary: MLMark uses real ML inference workloads but the supported models require far too much memory (GB-scale) and have significant runtimes for MCU-class devices, and it does not support power measurement.
items.notes: "the supported models are far too large for MCU-class devices...require far too much memory (GBs) and have significant runtimes... MLMark does not [support power measurement], which is critical for a TinyML benchmark."

items.summary: MLPerf's inference benchmark suite precludes MCUs and other resource-constrained platforms because it lacks small benchmarks and compatible implementations.
items.notes: "the current MLPerf inference benchmark precludes MCUs and other resource-constrained platforms due to a lack of small benchmarks and compatible implementations."

items.summary: Table 1 (v0.5 benchmark specification): KWS uses Speech Commands (49x10 input) with a DS-CNN model (52.5 KB) and a 90% Top-1 quality target; VWW uses the VWW Dataset (96x96) with MobileNetV1 (325 KB) and 80% Top-1; IC uses CIFAR10 (32x32) with a ResNet (96 KB) and 85% Top-1; AD uses ToyADMOS (5*128) with an FC-AutoEncoder (270 KB) and a 0.85 AUC target.

The suite targets model inference specifically and excludes pre- and post-processing from the measurement window. Reference implementations run the reference models as TFLite models using TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers on the NUCLEO-L4R5ZI board, built as a bare-metal MBED project with the GCC-ARM toolchain, and are open source on GitHub.

Visual wake words is included because person detection is directly relevant to smart-doorbell and occupancy applications, and the challenge's reference network fits on most 32-bit embedded microcontrollers.
items.notes: "This task is directly relevant to smart doorbell and occupancy applications, and the reference network provided as part of the challenge fits on most 32-bit embedded microcontrollers."

items.summary: VWW uses the MSCOCO 2014 dataset, preprocessed so training/validation/test images contain at least one person occupying more than 2.5% of the source image; images resized to 96x96.
VWW model: MobileNetV1 with alpha=0.25, 96x96 input images, two output classes (person / no person); the TFLM model is 325 KB.
The VWW reference model reaches about 86% accuracy across the preprocessed MSCOCO 2014 test dataset.
items.notes: "the model reaches about 86% accuracy across the preprocessed MSCOCO 2014 test dataset."

items.summary: The VWW closed-division accuracy threshold is set to at least 80% specifically to accommodate accuracy changes from quantization and rounding differences between platforms.
items.notes: "In order to accommodate changes in accuracy due to quantization and rounding differences between platforms, submissions to the closed category should reach at least 80% accuracy."

items.summary: Image classification is included because compact, low-cost, low-power, low-latency vision systems are spreading across manufacturing, IoT, and autonomous agents/vehicles, creating a need for a scientific and industrial point of reference.

CIFAR-10: 60,000 32x32x3 RGB images, 6,000 images per class, 10 classes (airplanes, cars, birds, cats, deer, dogs, frogs, horses, ships, trucks); divided into 5 training batches and 1 test batch of 10,000 images each.
CIFAR-10 was chosen partly to continue a documented trend of prior TinyML work using CIFAR-10, creating a point of reference that lets future results relate to historical data points.
items.notes: "A significant amount of prior work in TinyML has used CIFAR-10 as a target dataset [8], by continuing this trend, we create a point of reference in the benchmark suite that can be used to relate future results to historical data points."

items.summary: IC model: a custom ResNetv1 for 32x32x3 input and a 10-class output, with three residual stacks (versus four in the official ResNet) and fewer/lower-stride convolution filters than the official architecture; the TFLite model is 96 KB.
The IC model's first convolutional layer is not followed by a pooling layer, specifically because of the low resolution of the input data.
items.notes: "the first convolutional layer is not followed by the pooling layer due to the low resolution of the input data."

items.summary: The IC reference model reaches 86.5% accuracy across a 200-image subset of the CIFAR-10 test set, evaluated with the benchmark framework's runner software.
The IC quality target is set to 85% Top-1 accuracy specifically to accommodate minor differences from quantization and other optimizations.
items.notes: "To accommodate minor differences in quantization and various other optimizations, we set the quality target to 85% top-1 accuracy."

items.summary: Keyword spotting is included because wakeword detection requires continuous, low-power operation (a 100 mA current drain would deplete a typical phone battery in a day), and command-phrase recognition provides a simple, natural device interface; both need low latency and low power on small, low-cost devices.

Speech Commands v2: 105,829 utterances from 2,618 speakers, released under a Creative Commons BY license; 30 words plus background noise, split into train/validation/test so that any individual speaker appears in only one subset. 10 words are used directly; the remaining 20 words plus background noise are combined into an 'unknown' class; with 'silence' this gives 12 output classes.
The 12-class label design is meant to exercise both a command-phrase system's need to recognize multiple specific words and a wakeword system's need to reject an open set of background sounds.
items.notes: "This approach exercises a combination command-phrase systems' need for multiple words with wakeword systems' need for an open set of background noise."

items.summary: The KWS closed-division model, a small depthwise-separable CNN with 38.6K parameters, achieves 92.2% accuracy in the authors' experiments.

conditions.note: 'in our experiments'; dataset/split not further specified at this point in the text

items.summary: This KWS model was chosen because, at 38.6K parameters, it fits within the memory available on most microcontrollers and similarly-scaled devices, and because it uses standard layers that most neural-network hardware supports.

Feature extraction is excluded from the KWS measurement window, and three choices of pre-computed features are offered for the open division, because feature extraction is typically a small fraction of overall compute cost, so its impact on the measurement is judged minor.
items.notes: "we opted to exclude feature extraction from the measurement and provide three choices of pre-computed features for the open division. Feature extraction is typically a small fraction of the overall compute cost, so the impact on the measurements is minor."

items.summary: The quantized KWS reference model reaches 91.6% accuracy on the full Speech Commands test set and 91.7% on a randomly selected 1,000-utterance subset used for on-device evaluation.
The KWS accuracy requirement is set to 90% specifically to allow for slight variations in quantization strategy across platforms.

Anomaly detection is included because its unsupervised variant matters for industrial use cases (e.g., machine failure detection) where failure types are numerous and failure events rare, so training data is often available only for normal operation; sound captured by microphones is described as the most intuitive data source.

AD uses the DCASE2020 dataset, itself a combination of the ToyADMOS and MIMII datasets. The DCASE2020 competition covered six machine types (slide rail, fan, pump, valve, toy-car, toy-conveyor) with separate models allowed per type; MLPerf Tiny uses only the toy-car type. Training data: normal sound samples from seven different toy-cars, 1,000 samples each, mixing machine sound with environmental noise.
Only the toy-car machine type is used (rather than all six DCASE2020 types) because the authors judged that benchmarking would not benefit from that additional complexity.
items.notes: "Benchmarking would not benefit from this type of complexity, thus we choose to use the Toy-car machine type only."

items.summary: The AD autoencoder model was selected because it is the reference for a large part of the anomalous-sound-detection literature and thus a well-known baseline, and because it adds a new, fully-connected-only model type to the benchmark suite.

AD model architecture: input and output size of 640; both encoder and decoder are four 128-unit fully-connected layers with BatchNorm applied during training and ReLU activation; the bottleneck layer has size 8. Audio is preprocessed into a 128-band log-mel-spectrogram with a 32 ms frame size; the model is applied repeatedly over a sliding window of 5 frames (5x128=640); the MSE reconstruction error is averaged over the central 6.4-second part of the spectrogram to give an overall anomaly score.
AD is scored with the parameterless AUC-ROC metric rather than a metric requiring a chosen decision threshold, because AUC-ROC is judged to fit the quality evaluation of this problem better.
On an evaluation set of 248 samples (normal and anomalous sounds from four different machines), the fp32 AD reference model reaches an AUC of 0.88, falling to an AUC of 0.86 after quantization.
The AD benchmark's quality threshold of AUC 0.85 was set based directly on the fp32 (0.88) and quantized (0.86) AUC values.
items.notes: "Based on these two numbers, we've set the threshold for the benchmark to AUC 0.85."

items.summary: The suite uses a modular reference-implementation design specifically so that a submitter can demonstrate the competitive advantage of one specific component of the stack, rather than only whole-system results.
items.notes: "to enable users to demonstrate the competitive advantage of their specific contribution, we employ a modular approach to benchmark design."

items.summary: Closed-division rules: submissions must use the same models, datasets, and quality targets as the reference implementation; post-training quantization with the provided calibration data is permitted; retraining or weight replacement is prohibited.

Open-division rules: submitters may change the model, training scripts, and dataset; accuracy is still measured on the same test dataset, but meeting the closed-division accuracy threshold is not required; every deviation from the reference implementation must be documented.
The two-division design (closed and open) exists specifically to balance comparability against flexibility.
items.notes: "This two division design allows the benchmark to balance comparability and flexibility."

items.summary: Measurement procedure: (1) Latency -- five repeats, each downloading an input stimulus, loading the input tensor, running inference for a minimum of 10 seconds and 10 iterations, and measuring inferences per second (IPS); the median IPS of the five runs is reported as the score. (2) Accuracy -- a single inference pass over the entire set of validation inputs, from which Top-1 percent or AUC is computed; each model has a minimum accuracy that must be met for the score to be valid. (3) Energy -- identical to the latency procedure, but total energy in the timing window is also measured and converted to microjoules per inference; again the median of five measurements is used.

Only one power supply is allowed to power the device core during energy measurement -- no auxiliary batteries, supercapacitors, or energy harvesters -- specifically so that these cannot be used to defeat the measurement; power delivered to level-shifters is excluded from the score because it is a cost of the framework, not the device under test.
items.notes: "no additional energy supplies, such as batteries, supercapacitors, or energy harvesters may be used to defeat the measurement."

items.summary: A host-PC runner application is needed because the target platform typically has less than a megabyte of flash memory and cannot itself hold the input files needed for accuracy measurement; the runner supports three energy-monitor drivers (STMicroelectronics LPM01A, Jetperch Joulescope JS110, Keysight N6705).
The paper states that the four reference implementations, run on the NUCLEO-L4R5ZI board, covered a wide scope of latency and energy and each met its minimum accuracy target, illustrated in Figure 5.
items.notes: "Figure 5 illustrates the reference implementation results. The four benchmarks cover a wide scope in terms of latency and energy and each reference meets the minimum accuracy." The chart's underlying numeric values (specific IPS and microjoules/inference per benchmark) are not present in the extracted text -- only this qualitative summary and the caption survive extraction. See missing_evidence MISS-1.

items.summary: The first round of MLPerf Tiny submissions took place in June 2021 and is summarized in Table 2; results are listed publicly and each submission is reproducible from published instructions.

Table 2 lists five v0.5 submissions. Four in the closed division: (a) an ARM MCU running TensorFlow Lite Micro with INT-8 post-training quantization, demonstrating baseline performance on the reference platform; (b) a RISC-V MCU running TensorFlow Lite Micro with INT-8 PTQ, demonstrating a RISC-V microcontroller customized for neural-network inference; (c) a Raspberry Pi 4 running the LEIP Framework with FP-32 and INT-8 PTQ, demonstrating a hardware-agnostic software optimization toolchain; (d) a neural-network accelerator (Syntiant TDK) with INT-8 PTQ, demonstrating ultra-low-power hardware efficiency. One in the open division: an FPGA configured through QKeras/HLS4ML with Int-6/8 quantization-aware training, demonstrating rapid end-to-end development of ML accelerators on reconfigurable fabric.

rows.demonstrates: Baseline performance results on the reference platform.
Performance of a RISC-V microcontroller customized for neural network inference.
Capabilities of a software-only optimization toolchain that is agnostic of the hardware.
Ultra-low power hardware efficiency for running deep neural networks.
Rapid end-to-end development of machine learning accelerators on reconfigurable fabrics.

items.notes: The table caption states 'X indicates no modification...check mark indicates a modification', but no check-mark glyphs survived text extraction, so the fine-grained per-column (Dataset/Training/Model) modification pattern cannot be read with confidence beyond the Closed/Open division itself. See missing_evidence MISS-3. Per-submission numeric accuracy/latency/energy scores are not given in the paper text; see missing_evidence MISS-4.

items.summary: Across the v0.5 submissions: 8-bit integer was the most common numerical format for inference; ML frameworks ranged from an open-source interpreter (TFLite Micro) to hardware-specific inference compilers; platforms included MCUs, accelerators, and FPGAs; measured power consumption ranged from microwatts to watts.
items.notes: "the most common numerical format is 8-bit integer for inference as it offers a performance boost with little impact to the model accuracy." ... "The power consumption of these platforms ranged from µWatts to Watts."

items.summary: Despite a general trend in AI toward data-centric design, none of the submissions in the first round modified the training dataset.
items.notes: "despite a general trend in AI towards data-centric design, none of the submissions in the first round modified the training dataset."

items.summary: Four per-submitter narratives are given: an SDK vendor demonstrating hardware-agnostic developer tools that optimize NN inference for compute/energy/memory while preserving accuracy; a hardware vendor demonstrating an NN accelerator's efficiency via a microarchitecture/datapath design that avoids wait-states; an academic research institute demonstrating RISC-V-based AI microcontroller compute capability; and a multidisciplinary team showcasing the open-source 'hls4ml' workflow, originally built for sub-microsecond ML inference at the Large Hadron Collider and aimed more broadly at low-power-to-high-performance accelerator design.

The paper states that the benchmarks have already acted as a standard set of tasks for TinyML research (citing ref [4]) and have been made into public projects on a TinyML development platform (citing ref [16]).
items.notes: "The benchmarks have already acted as a standard set of tasks for TinyML research [4] and have been made into public projects on a TinyML development platform [16]."

items.summary: The authors note that TinyML could democratize AI and preserve privacy, but the same technology could be misused to track or monitor unwilling individuals, and inexpensive devices can lead to increased electronic waste.
items.notes: "the technology could be misused to more efficiently track and monitor unwilling individuals. Furthermore, because the devices themselves are inexpensive, TinyML can lead to increased electronic waste."

items.summary: The authors state that the suite will need to keep evolving with new benchmarks for new application domains, while also needing long-term stability so it can track historical progress; they mention keeping the benchmark open source and keeping a stable subset for this purpose.
items.notes: "MLPerf Tiny will continue to evolve to reflect the needs of the community. This will include new benchmarks that target new applications domains, such as wearables, medical devices, and environmental monitoring... This latter goal requires benchmarks to be stable over time... we also envision a subset of benchmarks to be kept long-term stable for this purpose."

items.summary: The authors state that streaming and pre-processing are unresolved measurement issues: bandwidth limits between the runner and the device under test make streaming hard to reproduce faithfully, excluding feature extraction while letting submitters vary it risks a degenerate 'whole model is feature extraction' case, and including it would over-weight its cost in a non-streaming benchmark; they aim to widen scope to pre-processing in future versions.
items.notes: "Excluding feature extraction from measurement while allowing submitter-selected variations in feature extraction creates the possibility of a degenerate case where an entire model up to the penultimate layer is defined as 'feature extraction'. Rigidly defined feature extraction precludes joint optimization over feature and model architecture that can be critical in the constrained systems targeted by this benchmark suite... In future versions, we aim to widen the scope of the benchmarks to include pre-processing as well."

items.summary: The authors state that the closed division currently supports only FC and CNN layers in well-known architectures, and that future benchmarks may add other architectures such as RNNs.

locator.anchor: Section 8 Limitations, 'Extended coverage of layer types and model architectures'

items.notes: "The closed division of the current benchmark suite includes models based mainly on FC and CNN layers in a variety of well known architectures, allowing only open division submissions to deviate from these... future benchmarks may include reference implementations using additional architectures e.g. RNNs."

items.summary: The project README describes target TinyML hardware (microcontrollers, DSPs, tiny NN accelerators) as typically running between 10 MHz and 250 MHz and performing inference using less than 50 mW of power.

The README's version table shows releases beyond the v0.5 paper: v0.5 (2021-06-16), v0.7 (2022-04-06), v1.0 (2022-11-09), v1.1 (2023-06-27), with a further round (v1.2) anticipated (submission deadline stated as 2024-03-15, not finalized per the README).

The authors state directly that there is a clear and distinct need for a TinyML benchmark that treats power as a first-class citizen and prescribes a methodology suited to TinyML, summarized by Table 1.
items.notes: "As Table 1 summarizes, there is a clear and distinct need for a TinyML benchmark that caters to the unique needs of ML workloads, makes power a first-class citizen and prescribes a methodology that suits TinyML."

items.summary: The authors' own interpretation of the first submission round: TinyML design is still largely focused on models, frameworks, and hardware rather than data; they anticipate this will shift in future rounds, and conclude the round shows the benchmark 'meets a variety of needs.'
items.notes: "While we anticipate this will shift in future versions, TinyML design is still largely focused on models, frameworks, and hardware. To this end, as demonstrated, the benchmark meets a variety of needs."

items.summary: The authors state directly, in the abstract, that continued progress in TinyML is limited by the lack of a widely accepted and easily reproducible benchmark for these systems.
items.notes: "However, continued progress is limited by the lack of a widely accepted and easily reproducible benchmark for these systems."
